text: Chapters 1 and 2 taught you to wire a tool straight into your own agent. But at scale, every AI application that wants GitHub issues, Slack messages, or a database query ends up writing its own bespoke integration for each service -- the same glue code, rebuilt over and over.

M applications and N services means M times N separate integrations. The Model Context Protocol, created by Anthropic and now maintained as an open standard, fixes that: a service builds one MCP server, and any MCP-compatible app -- Claude, ChatGPT, an IDE, your own agent -- connects to it the same way.

MCP's own docs put it simply: it's a USB-C port for AI applications. USB-C didn't add capability, it standardized how devices connect. MCP does the same for AI apps and the tools, data, and workflows they need -- already supported across real clients and servers today.

None of these are new capabilities -- an agent could already check a calendar or query a database the Chapter 2 way. What's new is the integration itself gets built once, and works with every MCP-compatible host instead of just one.

A tool exposed by an MCP server still has a name, description, and input schema -- exactly Lesson 6's format. What MCP adds is a standardized way to discover and call those tools. Next up: the three participants, host, client, and server, that make a connection actually work.
